name: Aisha Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and what you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Fieldwork, a five-person studio that only does work for charities and nonprofits. Today, for example, I was laying out a food bank's annual report and making posters for a housing charity's winter appeal. Ruth, who founded the place, does the big ideas, and I do a lot of the turning-it-into-pages. I like that the work means something, even if the budgets are tiny.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Charity committees. You send one logo and get eleven sets of comments, and three of them contradict each other. I'm also still slow at the technical side, print settings and file prep, and Jun, the middle-weight designer, has to check my files before anything goes to the printer. I use an AI tool now and then for quick mock-ups, but I don't trust it with anything final.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's nice that the hype calmed down, but the real problem was never the robots, it was funding. I'd probably post something about how charities still need real designers who understand the people they serve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job still isn't secure, it just isn't threatened by AI. Two of our charity clients lost government grants this year, and when that happens, design is the first thing they stop paying for. The quick-resize jobs that AI takes are also the jobs Ruth gave me to learn on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the mock-up tool when it saves time, and spend the rest of the year getting better at print prep so Jun doesn't have to check everything. I'd keep the four months of savings we've got and try to add a bit. And I'd sign up for the creative workers' union, which I keep meaning to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think. Not scared, but aware that the ground under small studios is always a little soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the budgets are tiny. What happens if a client pulls out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth has said that if we lose one more big client, she'd go to four-day weeks for everyone. Losing a day's pay would mean I couldn't put anything aside, and our rent on Lark Street went up in September. We'd survive, but it would sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomás about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Tomás that teaching looks like the stable job in our house now, which is funny because he's always the one complaining. He'd say I should apply to the in-house team at the city council. I'd say I'd rather work for charities, and we'd have that argument again.

say: I'd say the **real problem** for designers is charity funding, not robots.
I'd post that charities still need designers who **understand people**.
think: My job isn't secure, because **lost grants** make design the first thing charities cut.
The **small jobs** AI takes are the ones juniors learn on.
do: Get better at **print prep** so Jun stops checking every file.
Add to the **four months** of savings and finally join the creative workers' union.
feel: **Uneasy**, aware that small studios always stand on soft ground.
S0.quote: My job still isn't secure, it just isn't threatened by AI.
fieldNote: Her worry is **funding**, not technology, even in the calm scenario.
A **four-day week** at Fieldwork would wipe out her saving.
She and Tomás have a running **argument** about council versus charity work.

steps.text: Keep designing reports and appeals for Fieldwork's charity clients
Add to the four months of savings each month
Join the creative workers' union this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules: AI companies shouldn't be able to train on designers' work for free, and studios that cut staff should have to help them retrain. I'd share the union's statements and probably go to a meeting or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the obvious person to cut. Laying out a report from a template, writing alt text, resizing posters, that's most of my week and it's exactly the kind of thinking work these tools get good at first. My boss Ruth won't sack me out of meanness, she'd do it because a charity asks why the annual report costs twice what the software would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ruth to let me take on the accessibility checks, making sure our reports work for people with sight problems, because that needs judgment and talking to real users. I'd do an evening course in accessible design over the winter, maybe two hundred and fifty out of savings. I'd also start using the AI tools properly for the layout grunt work, so I'm the junior who's fast, not the junior who's replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's tilting slowly. Not falling, just tilting, and I'm at the low end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. Would you use them more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but carefully. I'd use them for the boring parts, like setting up the grid and the first rough layout, and check everything they make, because a charity can't afford a poster that misspells the helpline number. I've seen Jun use one for colour palettes and it's honestly fine for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Fieldwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jun, a little, but mostly me and Dami, our part-time copywriter. Dami's whole job is turning a charity's notes into readable text, and that's the first thing these tools do well. She's a single mum, so for her it's not an abstract question.

I'd say studios that cut staff should **fund retraining**, and I'd share union statements.
think: Template layouts, alt text and resizing are **most of my week**.
Ruth wouldn't cut me from meanness but because **charities compare costs**.
do: Ask Ruth to give her the **accessibility checks** on every report.
Pay about **250** for an evening accessible design course this winter.
Use AI tools for **layout grunt work** to stay the fast junior.
feel: Like the floor is **tilting** slowly, with her at the low end.
S1.quote: My boss Ruth won't sack me out of meanness, she'd do it because a charity asks why the annual report costs twice what the software would.
fieldNote: She blames **pricing pressure**, not her boss, for any cuts.

steps.text: Use AI tools for report grids and rough layouts, checking every result
Take an evening accessible design course this winter
Go to creative workers' union meetings and share their statements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a crisis and governments need to treat it like one: income support, a pause on layoffs while people retrain, something. I'd be at protests, honestly. It wouldn't feel like a debate about technology any more, it'd feel like a debate about who gets to eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think design as a job I could get hired for is finished by 2028. Fieldwork might survive as Ruth and a subscription. Everything I do happens on a screen, so I don't even get the three extra years the robots take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the course money and push savings from four months toward six straight away. I'd talk to Tomás about whether we can live on his teacher's salary for a year if we move somewhere cheaper. And I'd look hard at work that's with people in a room, like running community workshops for the charities we already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and sort of grieving. I only got into this job three years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the thinking parts go in 2028. Is there any part of your job that lasts longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the bits where I'm physically with people, like when we run a workshop at the food bank to ask volunteers what they want on the posters. I don't think a machine stands in a church hall with tea and biscuits in 2028. But that's an afternoon a month, not a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, then my gym, then the car share. If it's really bad, we'd move out of Lark Street to somewhere near Tomás's school, which is cheaper anyway. We'd also stop talking about kids for a while, which we'd only just started doing.

say: I'd call it a **crisis** needing income support and a pause on layoffs.
I'd join **protests**, because it becomes a debate about who gets to eat.
think: Design as a **hireable job** is finished for me by 2028.
Everything she does is **on a screen**, so the robot delay doesn't help.
do: Stop course spending and push savings toward **six months**.
Plan with Tomás to live on his **teacher's salary** somewhere cheaper.
Look for **in-person work** like community workshops with existing charity clients.
feel: **Frightened**, and grieving a career only three years old.
S2.quote: I don't think a machine stands in a church hall with tea and biscuits in 2028.
fieldNote: She sees no **robot buffer** because her whole job is screen work.
The only lasting part is **in-person workshops**, an afternoon a month.
The fast version pauses **talk of children** with Tomás.

steps.text: Push savings from four months toward six
Join protests for income support and a pause on layoffs
Pitch community design workshops to Fieldwork's charity clients
Put plans for children on hold and consider moving near Tomás's school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've had a warning and we should use it: retraining money, rules on AI in public services, and unions at the table. I'd be one of the people organising, because waiting for someone else clearly doesn't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my design work is gone by 2031, but five years is enough to move sideways. I'd want to be the person who talks to the people a charity serves and checks that what the AI makes actually works for them. That's a job, maybe, for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd take the accessibility course and then a user research course, maybe six hundred total over two years. I'd ask Ruth to send me on every client workshop. And I'd keep using the tools every week, so I understand what they get wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It feels like I'd be racing, but at least I'd be allowed to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more than now, because you can't check something you don't understand. I'd still hate the idea that they were built on other people's work without asking. Both of those can be true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use the AI tools in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be twenty-nine and ideally doing research for charities, maybe at a bigger one in-house. I don't know if those jobs exist after 2031 either. Nobody does.

I'd help **organise**, because waiting for others doesn't work.
think: My design work is gone by 2031, but five years lets me **move sideways**.
I'd aim to **check AI work** against what real people need.

fieldNote: She frames the extra time as a chance to **move sideways**, not stay put.

steps.text: Take accessibility and user research courses over two years
Use AI tools weekly on Fieldwork projects to learn their mistakes
Help organise the creative workers' union locally

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say there are no excuses: every government should have a plan for retraining and income support. I'd keep pushing that through the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a real career change. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI arrives, and I could have years as a researcher or even run accessibility testing for charities. Tomás's teaching gets three more years because it's half hands-on, so our house has a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the courses over two or three years and try for an in-house research role at a bigger charity by about 2030. I'd keep saving a little each month. I'd stay at Fieldwork while it lasts, because Ruth has been good to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. It's still the end of the job I trained for, but it's an ending I can walk out of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound calmer. Is that fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. With two years I'm a casualty, but with ten years I'm someone who changed careers, which loads of people do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the decade go well for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting in-house before the rush, honestly. And the union winning some kind of transition fund, so I'm not paying for all of the retraining out of my own savings.

I'd keep pushing for **retraining and income** support through the union.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be thrown out before I could become anything else. What would help is income support for a year while you retrain, paid for by the companies that made the tools. And the courses being free, not six hundred out of my own pocket.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who'll design for poor people. Charities will use whatever's cheapest, and I worry the people we serve end up with worse, cheaper stuff that nobody checked. Somebody needs to stand in the church hall and ask the volunteers.

headlineQuote: Charities will use whatever's cheapest, and I worry the people we serve end up with worse, cheaper stuff that nobody checked.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old junior designer** at Fieldwork, a five-person studio working only for charities.
She uses AI tools **now and then** and lives with Tomás, a teacher.
Her **progressive views** mean she pushes for rules, unions and retraining paid by AI firms.
Her plan is to move sideways into **accessibility and user research**.
Ten years' warning turns her from **casualty** into career-changer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be pushed out before becoming anything else.
whatWouldHelp: A year of **income support** while retraining, paid for by AI companies.
**Free courses** instead of paying from her own savings.
